title: NSFNET backbone → commercial Internet backbones
summary: NSFNET, which NSF launched in 1986 to link researchers to its supercomputer centers, became the de facto U.S. Internet backbone. From 1990 it was run by Advanced Network & Services (ANS), a nonprofit formed by NSF's awardee Merit Network and its partners IBM and MCI. Under solicitation NSF 93-52, NSF replaced the backbone with a new design: Network Access Points run by Sprint, MFS Datanet, Ameritech and Pacific Bell where commercial networks interconnect, a research-only vBNS run by MCI, and a routing arbiter run by Merit and USC. It also paid regional networks, on a declining scale, to buy service from commercial providers. The NSFNET backbone was shut down at midnight on April 30, 1995. Congress had authorized NSF in 1992 to support networks that also carry non-research traffic.

links.claim: NSF describes shutting down its backbone in 1995 as 'the decommissioning of NSFNET and privatization of the internet', and Merit, the backbone's awardee, says the NSFNET Backbone was retired in April 1995 and replaced by a set of commercial providers.

Through Program Solicitation NSF 93-52, NSF selected MFS Datanet (Washington, DC), Sprint (New York) and Bellcore (for NAPs in California run by PacBell and Chicago run by Ameritech) to operate Network Access Points; Sprint's NAP cooperative agreement began July 1, 1994, with $573,577 obligated.

claims.claim: The government sold the Internet backbone to private companies in 1995.
claims.explanation: No government sale of the backbone was found. NSF shut its backbone service down and paid for a new design in which commercial carriers interconnect at NSF-funded Network Access Points, while a separate research network (vBNS) was contracted to MCI. The network that had carried NSFNET was run by ANS, a nonprofit formed by IBM, MCI and Merit. AOL, not the government, announced in November 1994 that it would buy ANS for $35 million.

claims.claim: NSF let commercial traffic onto the taxpayer-funded backbone without legal authority or oversight.
claims.explanation: The NSF Office of Inspector General reviewed the NSFNET program and recommended fixes for deficiencies. NSF then wrote the acceptable use policy into the award to ensure commercial use did not impair research and education use. In October 1992 Congress (Pub. L. 102-476) authorized NSF to support access to networks used for other purposes as well, provided this increased their overall capacity to support research and education.
